title: Inference
lede: API-based vs self-hosted inference; vLLM, TGI, SGLang, Ollama, llama.cpp; GGUF/AWQ/GPTQ/INT4-INT8 quantisation; KV cache, prefix caching, speculative decoding; continuous batching; TTFT vs TPS; GPU economics, edge inference, and the major hosted providers (Together, Fireworks, Groq, Cerebras, Replicate, AWS Bedrock). Each section ships in two voices: the engineer's version (technical, with code & diagrams) and a layman's version (plain English with analogies). প্রতিটি টপিকের শেষে বাংলা ব্যাখ্যাও আছে।

sections.title: Inference (servers, quantization, providers)
sections.sub: Every LLM call has two sides: the request you send and the inference that serves it. Most teams start by renting (Together, Fireworks, Groq, Cerebras, Replicate, AWS Bedrock). Once usage justifies it, you self-host with vLLM, TGI, SGLang, Ollama, or llama.cpp — and learn a different optimization vocabulary: KV cache, prefix caching, speculative decoding, continuous batching.

rows: Anything you can fit on your GPU

blocks.html: Rule of thumb: start hosted. Move to self-hosting once your bill exceeds the cost of a half-time ML engineer plus two H100s.

body.html: When you self-host, an inference server is the process that loads model weights into GPU memory and serves requests. The five that matter in 2025:

blocks.html: The throughput champion. PagedAttention + continuous batching typically deliver 10–24× the throughput of naive Hugging Face.[13] Python API + OpenAI-compatible HTTP server.
Hugging Face's Rust+Python server. Polished, supports the HF model hub natively, slightly lower raw TPS than TGI/vLLM.
Optimised for structured-output and multi-call programs (RadixAttention for prefix caching across calls).[14]
One-line CLI for local laptops and small servers. Best for dev and small-scale prod.
CPU-first, GGUF-native, runs on phones and Raspberry Pis. Foundation for most edge inference.[15]
NVIDIA's compiled kernels for maximum H100 throughput. Most ops effort, best raw TPS.

body.html: Quantization reduces the precision of model weights from 16-bit to 8- or 4-bit, trading a small amount of quality for 2–4× less GPU memory and proportionally faster inference. The common formats:

items: GGUF — llama.cpp's format. Single file, CPU+GPU hybrid, the de facto standard for open-weight local inference.[15]
AWQ — Activation-aware Weight Quantization. 4-bit with near-FP16 quality; popular for vLLM/SGLang.[16]
GPTQ — older, still common for GPU serving.
INT8 / FP8 — minimal-quality-loss quantisation on H100s; native hardware support.
INT4 / NF4 — bitsandbytes (QLora) for training; also used at inference time.

body.html: KV cache, prefix caching, speculative decoding
Three ideas that show up in every modern inference server:

items: Paged KV cache: instead of one contiguous buffer per request, KV cache memory is allocated in pages (à la OS virtual memory). vLLM's PagedAttention removes the wasted-memory problem of naive serving.[13]

Prefix caching: if many requests share a long system prompt, the server hashes the prefix and reuses the cached KV. Anthropic's prompt_caching and OpenAI's cached_prompt save 80–90% of cost on the cached portion.[17]
Speculative decoding: a tiny draft model proposes the next 5–10 tokens; the big model verifies them in parallel. Net throughput +2–3× for free, no quality loss.

body.html: Naive serving processes one request at a time per GPU. Continuous batching (vLLM, TGI, SGLang) interleaves tokens from many requests so the GPU is never idle waiting for one slow request. This alone typically delivers 5–20× higher throughput.[13] Add max_num_seqs, max_model_len, and CUDA-graph capture for the next 2×.

rows: How long until the user sees the first word
Model size, batch size, KV-cache hits

body.html: GPU economics, edge inference, on-device models

An H100 rents for $2–$4/hr on the major clouds, ~$30k to buy. At a 70B model, you serve ~30 concurrent requests before latency collapses — about $0.10 per 1k generated tokens fully loaded. Edge inference pushes smaller models onto the user's device (3B–8B on phones via MLX, llama.cpp, or vendor SDKs).[15] The trade-off: zero server cost, but quality and capability are limited.
Hosted inference in 2025 is a commodity market. Pick by which model you want at what price with what SLA:

layman.html: Two ways to run an AI: rent it, or own it.

• Renting (OpenAI, Anthropic, Together, Fireworks): you pay per request. No setup, no maintenance. Like taking the bus.
• Owning (vLLM on your own GPU): you buy (or rent) a powerful chip, install the software, and run the AI yourself. Like owning a car.
Start with renting. Switch to owning only when the bus fare is more than a car payment. For most companies, renting stays cheaper for years.

The "engine" matters when you own. If you do own, the inference server is the software that turns user requests into GPU math. The five big names in 2025 are vLLM (fastest for big loads), TGI (easy and from Hugging Face), SGLang (best when you reuse the same prompt a lot), Ollama (one-liner for your laptop), and llama.cpp (runs on phones and Raspberry Pis).

Quantisation = "shrinking the AI without ruining it." A full-size AI model takes 16 GB of memory. Quantise it to 4-bit and it takes 4 GB — losing maybe 1% of quality. For most apps you don't notice. This is why your phone can now run a chat AI offline.
Three magic tricks that make serving fast:

• KV cache — the AI remembers what it already computed instead of redoing the math. Like a calculator that holds the previous answer.
• Prefix caching — if 1,000 users all start with the same system prompt ("You are a customer-service agent for Acme Inc…"), the AI computes that once and reuses it. Saves 80%+ on the cached part.
• Speculative decoding — a tiny draft model guesses the next word, the big model checks. Both run at once. Net speedup 2–3× with zero quality loss.

Latency vs throughput — the eternal trade-off. Latency = how fast one user gets their first word (TTFT). Throughput = how many total users the system can serve at once. Continuous batching is the trick that lets you serve 50 users at once with barely more latency than serving 5. It's the difference between "one customer at a time at the deli counter" and "one big batch of soup."

GPU economics: an H100 chip costs ~$30k to buy, or $2–4/hour to rent. At full tilt it serves ~30 conversations at once. So if you're running millions of conversations, owning is cheaper. If you're running thousands, renting is cheaper.

blocks.html: The bus-vs-car analogy: taking the bus (OpenAI, Anthropic, Together) is cheaper when you're one passenger. Owning a car (self-hosting with vLLM) is cheaper when you're a taxi driver. But the car needs fuel (GPUs), maintenance (an ops engineer), and parking (a server room). Quantisation is like taking the engine apart and removing every fourth piston — the car still drives, just slightly less powerfully. KV caching is like remembering your route home so you don't have to re-look-up every turn.

bangla.html: দুটি পথ: API-ভিত্তিক inference (Together, Fireworks, Groq, Cerebras, Replicate, OpenAI, Anthropic) অথবা স্ব-হোস্টেড inference (vLLM, TGI, SGLang, Ollama, llama.cpp দিয়ে)। বেশিরভাগ দল আগে host করা API দিয়ে শুরু করে; বিল যথেষ্ট বড় হলে স্ব-হোস্টে যায়। সেই ক্ষেত্রে KV cache, prefix caching, speculative decoding, continuous batching — এই vocabulary শিখতে হয়।

items: vLLM — throughput চ্যাম্পিয়ন; PagedAttention + continuous batching সাধারণত ১০–২৪× উচ্চতর throughput দেয়।[13]
TGI — Hugging Face-এর Rust+Python server।
SGLang — structured-output ও multi-call program-এর জন্য অপ্টিমাইজড; RadixAttention prefix caching।[14]
Ollama — লোকাল ল্যাপটপ ও ছোট server-এর জন্য এক-লাইনের CLI।
llama.cpp — CPU-first, GGUF-native, ফোন ও Raspberry Pi-তেও চলে।[15]
TensorRT-LLM / Triton — NVIDIA-র compiled kernel; সর্বোচ্চ H100 throughput, সবচেয়ে বেশি ops প্রচেষ্টা।

bangla.html: Quantisation: weight precision ১৬-বিট থেকে ৮ বা ৪ বিটে নামানো, যাতে GPU memory ২–৪× কমে এবং inference আনুপাতিকভাবে দ্রুত হয়, সামান্য মান কমে। সাধারণ ফর্ম্যাট:

items: GGUF — llama.cpp-এর ফর্ম্যাট, single file, CPU+GPU hybrid, open-weight লোকাল inference-এর মানদণ্ড।[15]
AWQ — ৪-বিটে FP16-এর কাছাকাছি মান; vLLM/SGLang-এ জনপ্রিয়।[16]
GPTQ — পুরোনো, GPU serving-এ এখনও প্রচলিত।
INT8 / FP8 — H100-এ নেটিভ hardware support সহ সর্বনিম্ন মান-ক্ষতি।
INT4 / NF4 — bitsandbytes (QLoRA) প্রশিক্ষণে; inference-এও ব্যবহৃত।

bangla.html: তিনটি মন্ত্র যা প্রতিটি আধুনিক server-এ থাকে:

items: Paged KV cache: প্রতিটি request-এর জন্য একটি contiguous buffer-এর বদলে KV cache memory পেজে (OS virtual memory-র মতো) বরাদ্দ করা হয়।[13]

Prefix caching: অনেক request একই দীর্ঘ system prompt শেয়ার করলে server prefix hash করে KV পুনরায় ব্যবহার করে। Anthropic-এর prompt_caching ও OpenAI-র cached_prompt cached অংশে ৮০–৯০% খরচ বাঁচায়।[17]
Speculative decoding: একটি ছোট draft model পরবর্তী ৫–১০ token প্রস্তাব করে; বড় model সেগুলো সমান্তরালে যাচাই করে। গুণমান না কমিয়ে throughput ২–৩×।

bangla.html: Continuous batching: naive serving GPU-তে একবারে একটি request প্রক্রিয়া করে। Continuous batching (vLLM, TGI, SGLang) অনেক request-এর token আন্তঃপ্রবিষ্ট করে যাতে একটি slow request-এর জন্য GPU কখনো নিষ্ক্রিয় না হয়। এটাই এককভাবে ৫–২০× বেশি throughput দেয়।[13]

Latency বনাম throughput (TTFT, TPS): TTFT (time to first token) হলো ব্যবহারকারী কত তাড়াতাড়ি প্রথম শব্দ দেখে। TPS (tokens per second, per request) হলো generation-এর গতি যা ব্যবহারকারী দেখে। Aggregate throughput হলো server মোট কত token নিঃসরণ করে। p99 latency হলো সবচেয়ে খারাপ ১%।

GPU economics, edge inference, on-device models: H100 প্রধান cloud-এ ঘণ্টায় $2–$4-এ ভাড়া নেওয়া যায়, কিন্তু কেনা ~$30k। ৭০B মডেলে এটি latency ভেঙে পড়ার আগে প্রায় ৩০ সমকালীন request সার্ভ করে — পুরো লোডে প্রায় $0.10/১k generated token। Edge inference ছোট মডেল (৩B–৮B) ব্যবহারকারীর ডিভাইসে ঠেলে দেয় (MLX, llama.cpp বা vendor SDK দিয়ে)।[15]

Inference providers (২০২৫): Together (open-weight catalogue, ভালো default), Fireworks (দ্রুত, function-calling-optimised), Groq (LPU hardware, ultra-low latency), Cerebras (wafer-scale chip), Replicate (pay-per-second, model marketplace), AWS Bedrock / Azure AI Foundry (enterprise compliance), OpenRouter (aggregator)।

blocks.html: বাস বনাম গাড়ির উপমা: API inference হলো বাসে যাতায়াত (OpenAI, Anthropic, Together)। আপনি একজন যাত্রী হলে সস্তা। স্ব-হোস্ট (vLLM) হলো গাড়ি কেনা। ট্যাক্সি চালক হলে গাড়ি সস্তা, কিন্তু জ্বালানি (GPU), মেইনটেন্যান্স (ops ইঞ্জিনিয়ার) ও পার্কিং (server room) লাগে। কোয়ান্টাইজেশন হলো ইঞ্জিন খুলে প্রতি চতুর্থ পিস্টন বাদ দেওয়া — গাড়ি এখনও চলে, শুধু কম শক্তিতে। KV caching হলো বাড়ি ফেরার রাস্তা মনে রাখা, যাতে প্রতিটি মোড়ে আবার ম্যাপ না দেখতে হয়।

practice.title: Decide: hosted API or self-host
practice.goal: Do the cost math for a real-looking scenario and see when self-hosting starts to pay off.
steps: Read the scenario in Prompt A. On paper, work out the monthly cost of both options and guess the break-even traffic.
Start a new chat. Send Prompt A. Compare the model's numbers with yours. Fix any mistake by hand.
In the same chat, send Prompt B. Read the new recommendation and the reasons it gives.

prompts.label: Prompt A
prompts.text:
Scenario (all numbers are invented):
A small company, ShopLink, runs a customer-support chatbot. It uses 2 billion tokens per month.

Option 1, hosted API: 0.50 USD per 1 million tokens.
Option 2, self-host: rent 2 GPUs at 3 USD per hour each, 730 hours per month, plus a half-time ML engineer at 3,000 USD per month. Ignore the small per-token cost of electricity and storage.

Tasks:
1. Compute the monthly cost of each option. Show the arithmetic.
2. Compute the break-even: how many tokens per month make both options cost the same?
3. List 3 hidden costs of self-hosting that I did not include.
Reply with a short table, then a bullet list.

prompts.label: Prompt B
prompts.text: Now the situation changes. ShopLink grows to 20 billion tokens per month. A new customer also says the chat text must never leave ShopLink's own servers. Using the same prices, and assuming the same 2 GPUs can handle the load, what do you recommend now, and why? Give the monthly cost of both options and answer in under 120 words.

lookFor: Hosted: 2,000 million tokens × 0.50 = 1,000 USD. Self-host: 2 × 3 × 730 = 4,380 USD for GPUs, plus 3,000 USD for the engineer, so 7,380 USD. At this traffic the hosted API is cheaper.
Break-even is about 14.8 billion tokens per month. Check whether the model got this right.
In Prompt B, the larger bill and the privacy rule both point to self-hosting. Most models say so.

check.question: Why do most teams start with a hosted API and move to self-hosting later?
check.answer: A hosted API gives a fast time to first token and the vendor handles scaling. Self-hosting has fixed costs (GPUs and an engineer), so it pays off only when the token bill is large, or when data privacy or full control matters.

practice.challenge: Change one number in Prompt A, for example make the GPUs idle half of the month, or use a 5 USD hosted price. Does the break-even move up or down? Predict first.

practice.title: Calculate model memory at 16, 8, 4 bits
practice.goal: See with simple math why quantization lets a big model fit on one GPU or a small model fit on a laptop.
steps: Before you ask, compute by hand: a 70 billion parameter model needs how many GB of weights at 16-bit, 8-bit, and 4-bit?
Start a new chat. Send Prompt A. Compare the model's table with your numbers.
In the same chat, send Prompt B. Decide yourself first, then read the answer.
Note what the model says about KV cache and quality. Is memory for weights the whole story?

prompts.label: Prompt A
prompts.text:
A language model has 70 billion parameters. Use this rule: weight memory in GB = parameters in billions × bits per weight ÷ 8.

Make a table of weight memory at 16-bit, 8-bit, and 4-bit. Then say which of these fit on one GPU with 80 GB of memory. Finally, in one sentence, say what other memory the server needs at run time besides the weights.

prompts.label: Prompt B
prompts.text: I want to run an 8 billion parameter model on my laptop. The laptop has 16 GB of RAM, and about 8 GB of it is free for the model. Using the same rule, which precision (16-bit, 8-bit, or 4-bit) can I use? Give the memory for each. Then tell me one risk of using the smallest precision.

lookFor: 70B model: 140 GB at 16-bit, 70 GB at 8-bit, 35 GB at 4-bit. Only 8-bit and 4-bit fit in 80 GB, and 8-bit leaves very little room.
8B model: 16 GB at 16-bit, 8 GB at 8-bit, 4 GB at 4-bit. The 4-bit one fits with room to spare.
The model should mention the KV cache and a small quality loss. Weights are not the whole memory use.

check.question: What does quantization change, and what is the trade-off?
check.answer: It lowers the precision of the weights, for example from 16-bit to 4-bit, so the model needs about 2–4× less memory and runs faster. The cost is a small quality loss for most workloads.

practice.challenge: Ask the model to suggest a 5-question test you could use to compare a 16-bit and a 4-bit version of the same model. Which kinds of questions would show a quality drop first?

practice.title: Estimate savings from prefix caching
practice.goal: Calculate how much a shared system prompt costs with and without prefix caching, and see what breaks the cache.
steps: Read Prompt A. Guess the saving: more than 50%, or less? Write your guess.
Start a new chat. Send Prompt A. Check the arithmetic by hand.
Before you send Prompt B, predict what goes wrong. Then send it in the same chat.
Compare the model's explanation with your prediction.

prompts.label: Prompt A
prompts.text:
A support bot gets 10,000 requests per day (all numbers are invented). Every request starts with the same system prompt of 3,000 tokens. The user message adds 100 tokens. Input tokens cost 1 USD per 1 million. Cached input tokens cost 0.10 USD per 1 million (a 90% discount).

Compute the daily input cost (1) without prefix caching and (2) with prefix caching, where the system prompt is cached. Show the arithmetic. Then give the saving as a percentage.

prompts.label: Prompt B
prompts.text: The team now changes the system prompt. The first line becomes: "Today is {current date and time}. The user's name is {name}." The rest stays the same 3,000 tokens. Prefix caching stops working well. Explain in 3 short sentences why, and show how to change the prompt so the cache works again.

lookFor: Without caching: 31 million tokens per day, so 31 USD. With caching: 3 USD for the cached part plus 1 USD for the new part, so 4 USD. The saving is about 87%.
Prompt B: the date and name change on every request, so the start of the prompt is never the same. The server cannot reuse the cached prefix.
The fix is to keep the fixed text first and put the changing text last.

check.question: Why must the shared part of the prompt come first?
check.answer: Prefix caching hashes the start of the prompt and reuses the stored KV cache only when the start matches exactly. Any change early in the prompt makes the whole prefix new, so there is no cache hit.

practice.challenge: Try 1,000 requests per day instead of 10,000. How does the daily saving change in USD? When is prefix caching not worth the effort?

practice.title: Match symptoms to inference metrics
practice.goal: Practise reading latency symptoms (TTFT, TPS, throughput, p99) and choosing the right fix.
steps: Read the four symptoms in Prompt A. On paper, name the metric and one fix for each.
Start a new chat. Send Prompt A. Compare each answer with yours.
Mark where you and the model differ. Decide who is right, using the table of metrics in the section.

prompts.label: Prompt A
prompts.text:
I run an LLM inference server. For each symptom, name the main metric that is bad (TTFT, TPS per request, aggregate throughput, or p99 latency) and choose ONE best fix from this list: prefix caching, continuous batching, speculative decoding, a shorter prompt, a smaller or quantized model, or more GPU capacity.

Symptoms:
1. Users send a 20,000-token document. They wait 6 seconds before the first word appears. After that, text streams fast.
2. Even with only one user on the server, text appears at 8 tokens per second, which feels slow.
3. The GPU is idle about 60% of the time. The server finishes one request completely before it starts the next. Total tokens per second for all users is low.
4. Most requests are fast, but the slowest 1% take 40 seconds when the queue is long.

Reply with a table: symptom number, metric, fix, and a reason in 12 words or fewer.

lookFor: Symptom 1 is TTFT (long prefill). A shorter prompt or prefix caching fits. Symptom 2 is per-request TPS. Speculative decoding or a smaller or quantized model fits.
Symptom 3 is aggregate throughput. Continuous batching is the standard fix. Symptom 4 is p99 latency from queue depth. More capacity fits.
Some symptoms allow more than one good fix. Look at whether the model gives a reason that matches the metric.

check.question: Why can a server have good throughput and still feel slow to one user?
check.answer: Throughput counts tokens per second for all users together. A user feels TTFT and per-request TPS, and the worst users feel p99. Heavy batching can raise throughput while some single requests wait longer.

practice.challenge: Make up a fifth symptom with two possible fixes. Ask the model which fix to try first and why. Do you agree with the order?
